questions.stem:
A laboratory studies a new antifungal in culture. Fungal cells exposed to the drug swell and lyse at the growing tips, and biochemical assay shows that incorporation of glucose polymers into the outer layer of the cell has stopped. Human cells in the same assay are unaffected, and the authors note that the targeted polymer has no counterpart in human cells.

This drug most likely belongs to which class?
choices: Polyenes
Azoles
Echinocandins
Allylamines
Pyrimidine analogs

explain.html:
A fungal cell has two layers that antifungal drugs aim at: a cell membrane whose sterol is ergosterol, and an outer cell wall built from proteins, beta-glucans and chitin. Most drug classes act on the membrane, either by blocking ergosterol synthesis (azoles, allylamines) or by binding the membrane and making it leaky (polyenes). Flucytosine works inside the cell on nucleic acid synthesis. The echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) are the class that hits the wall: they inhibit 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase, so beta-D-glucan cannot be laid down.

In this experiment, glucose polymers stop being built into the outer layer and the cells burst at their growing tips, which is a cell wall failure. Since beta-D-glucan has no human counterpart, human cells are unaffected, which is why this class is well tolerated.
explain.table:
ClassTargetExample
PolyenesInsert into the membrane and raise its permeabilityAmphotericin B
AzolesC14-alpha-demethylation of lanosterol (ergosterol synthesis)Fluconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole
Echinocandins1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase (cell wall)Caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin
AllylaminesSqualene epoxidase (ergosterol synthesis)Terbinafine
Pyrimidine analogsConverted to 5-fluorouracil, blocks DNA and RNA synthesisFlucytosine
why: Polyenes insert into the membrane and make it leaky; they do not stop glucose polymers from being built into the wall.
Azoles block lanosterol demethylation in the membrane sterol pathway, not wall glucan synthesis.
Allylamines inhibit squalene epoxidase, an early step in ergosterol synthesis, not the wall.
Flucytosine is converted to 5-fluorouracil and blocks DNA and RNA synthesis, which leaves the wall intact.
explain.takeaway: Echinocandins inhibit 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase, blocking a fungal cell wall polymer that human cells do not make.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the components of a fungal cell

rows.why: Polyenes insert into the membrane and make it leaky; they do not stop glucose polymers from being built into the wall.
rows.if_right: cells that leak contents after a drug binds ergosterol in the membrane

rows.why: Azoles block lanosterol demethylation in the membrane sterol pathway, not wall glucan synthesis.
rows.if_right: lanosterol accumulating while ergosterol falls

rows.why: Flucytosine is converted to 5-fluorouracil and blocks DNA and RNA synthesis, which leaves the wall intact.

questions.stem:
A 16-year-old wrestler has an itchy, scaling, ring-shaped patch on his groin and thickened, crumbling toenails. His younger brother has patchy hair loss with broken hairs on the scalp. Scrapings from each lesion show branching septate hyphae. Neither boy is immunocompromised, and both report sharing towels at home.

Which property of these fungi best explains the distribution of the lesions?
choices: Angioinvasion with distal tissue infarction
A polysaccharide capsule that resists phagocytosis
Formation of spherules filled with endospores
Secretion of keratinase, which degrades keratin
Conversion to a yeast form at body temperature in tissue

explain.html:
Fungal infections are classified by depth: cutaneous, subcutaneous and systemic. The cutaneous mycoses are caused by dermatophytes, which infect only the epidermis, hair and nails. They manage this because they secrete keratinase, an enzyme that degrades keratin, the protein of those tissues, so they stay in keratinized tissue rather than invading deeper. They are contagious by direct contact with infected hairs and skin cells. They are named by site: tinea capitis (scalp), tinea barbae (beard), tinea cruris (groin), tinea pedis (feet) and tinea unguium (nails).

The wrestler has tinea cruris and tinea unguium, and his brother has tinea capitis, all in healthy hosts who share towels. Infection confined to keratinized sites, with septate hyphae on scrapings, is the keratinase pattern.
why: Angioinvasion with infarction is Aspergillus in neutropenic hosts, not a superficial rash in healthy boys.
A polysaccharide capsule is the virulence factor of Cryptococcus, a yeast that disseminates to the brain.
Spherules filled with endospores are the tissue form of Coccidioides in the lung.
Conversion to yeast at body temperature describes dimorphic fungi such as Histoplasma, which cause systemic disease.
explain.takeaway: Dermatophytes secrete keratinase, which confines them to skin, hair and nails, and they spread by direct contact.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Introduce examples of common human pathogens with clinical correlates

rows.why: Angioinvasion with infarction is Aspergillus in neutropenic hosts, not a superficial rash in healthy boys.
rows.if_right: hemoptysis and lung nodules with a halo in a patient with leukemia

rows.why: A polysaccharide capsule is the virulence factor of Cryptococcus, a yeast that disseminates to the brain.
rows.if_right: an encapsulated yeast with a halo on India ink of cerebrospinal fluid

rows.why: Spherules filled with endospores are the tissue form of Coccidioides in the lung.
rows.if_right: pneumonia after desert exposure with spherules on biopsy

rows.why: Conversion to yeast at body temperature describes dimorphic fungi such as Histoplasma, which cause systemic disease.
rows.if_right: a fungus that grows as a mold at room temperature and a yeast in tissue

questions.stem:
A 67-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus has been in the hospital for 3 weeks after abdominal surgery. She has received broad-spectrum antibiotics for a postoperative infection and parenteral nutrition through a central venous catheter because of poor oral intake. She now has a temperature of 38.8 C (101.8 F), a pulse of 118/min, blood pressure of 86/50 mm Hg, and confusion. Blood cultures are growing budding yeast.

Which element of this patient's course contributed most directly to the bloodstream invasion by this organism?
choices: Her history of diabetes mellitus alone
The indwelling central venous catheter
The three-week length of her hospital stay
Her age over 65 years
The abdominal location of her surgery

explain.html:
Candidemia is the most common form of systemic candidiasis. Its risk factors fall into host factors (prematurity, pregnancy, diabetes, HIV, malignancy, transplantation) and exposures (antibiotics, corticosteroids, central venous catheters, chemotherapy, major abdominal surgery, parenteral nutrition, prolonged ICU stay). Of all these, candidemia occurs most frequently with an intravascular catheter. The catheter gives the yeast a direct route into the bloodstream and a surface to grow on. From the blood it can seed the kidney, spleen, liver, eye and heart. Removing the catheter along with antifungal therapy shortens the infection in non-neutropenic patients.

This woman has several risk factors, but the line delivering parenteral nutrition is the one that provides direct vascular access for budding yeast to reach the blood.
why: Diabetes raises risk but does not by itself give the yeast a route into the blood.
A long hospital stay increases exposure but is not the portal of entry.
Age over 65 is not a candidiasis risk factor, while the catheter is the direct portal into the blood.
Major abdominal surgery is a risk factor, but here it is less direct than the indwelling line.
explain.takeaway: Candidemia occurs most often with an intravascular catheter, which provides direct bloodstream access, and catheter removal plus antifungal therapy shortens infection.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Introduce examples of common human pathogens with clinical correlates

rows.why: Diabetes raises risk but does not by itself give the yeast a route into the blood.
rows.if_right: mucosal candidiasis in a diabetic patient with no line

rows.why: A long hospital stay increases exposure but is not the portal of entry.
rows.if_right: a patient whose only risk is a prolonged ICU stay

rows.why: Age over 65 is not a candidiasis risk factor, while the catheter is the direct portal into the blood.
rows.if_right: candidemia in a pre-term infant, where extreme age itself is the host risk factor

rows.why: Major abdominal surgery is a risk factor, but here it is less direct than the indwelling line.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man treated years ago for a cavitary lung infection has intermittent cough, hemoptysis, fatigue, and mild weight loss. Chest imaging shows a rounded mass sitting inside a pre-existing upper lobe cavity, with air around it. Sputum culture grows a mold with septate hyphae. He has a normal white blood cell count and no immunosuppression, and his radiographs have looked the same for a year.

Which description best fits this condition?
choices: Colonization of an existing cavity by a mold, forming a fungus ball
Hypersensitivity to airway colonization, with eosinophilia and high serum immunoglobulin E
Angioinvasive growth with infarction in a neutropenic host
Hematogenous seeding of the lung from an intravascular catheter
Granulomatous reaction to inhaled yeast residing in macrophages

explain.html:
Aspergillus causes three different lung diseases depending on the host. In asthma or cystic fibrosis it causes a hypersensitivity reaction (allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis). In profound neutropenia it invades vessels. In a lung with a pre-existing cavity or devitalized area, it can simply colonize the space and form a fungus ball, the aspergilloma. Imaging shows a round mass inside the cavity, and symptoms include cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, weight loss and fatigue. Patients with no symptoms and stable films need no therapy, and surgical resection is the definitive treatment for hemoptysis.

This man has an old cavity holding a rounded mass with air around it, a normal white count, no immunosuppression and films unchanged for a year. That is colonization, not invasion.
explain.table:
Aspergillus syndromeHostKey findingsTreatment
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosisAsthma or cystic fibrosisFleeting infiltrates, eosinophilia, high IgESteroids plus itraconazole or voriconazole
Aspergilloma (fungus ball)Pre-existing cavity, not immunosuppressedRound mass inside a cavity, hemoptysisNone if stable; resection for hemoptysis
Invasive aspergillosisProlonged profound neutropenia, transplantNodules, halo sign, infarctionAntifungal therapy
why: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis occurs in asthma or cystic fibrosis with fleeting infiltrates, not a stable mass in a cavity.
Angioinvasive disease occurs in profound neutropenia and progresses fast, unlike this stable picture.
Seeding from an intravascular catheter describes candidemia with organ involvement.
Granulomatous disease with yeast inside macrophages describes histoplasmosis, not a mold in a cavity.
explain.takeaway: An aspergilloma is a fungus ball colonizing a pre-existing lung cavity; it needs no therapy when stable, and resection treats hemoptysis.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Introduce examples of common human pathogens with clinical correlates

rows.if_right: an asthmatic with migrating infiltrates, eosinophilia and high IgE

rows.why: Angioinvasive disease occurs in profound neutropenia and progresses fast, unlike this stable picture.
rows.if_right: a neutropenic patient with new nodules and a halo sign

questions.stem:
Two patients have pulmonary infection with an encapsulated budding yeast. The first is an immunocompetent man who was part of an outbreak on Vancouver Island, where the organism was recovered from eucalyptus trees. The second is a worker who was demolishing an old building where pigeons had roosted for years.

Which statement about these two organisms is correct?
choices: Both species are routinely cultured from bird droppings
The Vancouver Island species has a limited geographic distribution
The pigeon species is found only in the Pacific Northwest
Neither species disseminates beyond the lungs
Both species lack a capsule and show broad-based budding

explain.html:
Two Cryptococcus species cause human disease, and they differ mainly in their environmental source and geography. C. neoformans is the main human pathogen, and pigeon excreta are its most common source. Lung infection has occurred in workers demolishing old buildings where pigeons had roosted. C. gattii has never been cultured from bird guano; it is linked to eucalyptus trees and has a limited geographic range, including the outbreak on Vancouver Island in British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest. Both are encapsulated yeasts that start as lung infections, and both can disseminate, most often to the meninges.

The Vancouver Island patient fits C. gattii, and the demolition worker fits C. neoformans.
explain.table:
FeatureC. neoformansC. gattii
SourcePigeon excretaEucalyptus trees, never bird guano
GeographyWorldwideLimited (Vancouver Island, Pacific Northwest)
DiseaseLung infection, then meningitisLung infection, then meningitis
why: C. gattii has never been cultured from bird guano, so this cannot apply to both.
The pigeon species, C. neoformans, occurs widely; it is C. gattii whose range is limited.
Both species can disseminate from the lungs, most often to the meninges.
Both species are encapsulated yeasts; broad-based budding describes Blastomyces.
explain.takeaway: C. neoformans comes from pigeon excreta worldwide, while C. gattii is linked to eucalyptus trees, has a limited range and is never found in bird guano.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Introduce examples of common human pathogens with clinical correlates

questions.stem:
Five patients living in the same southwestern desert county are diagnosed with primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis in the same month. The clinic is deciding which patients need closer follow-up for spread beyond the lungs. The patients are a 28-year-old in the third trimester of pregnancy, a 30-year-old marathon runner, a 24-year-old graduate student, a 35-year-old smoker with no other illness, and a 40-year-old with seasonal allergies.

Which patient is at greatest risk for disseminated disease?
choices: The graduate student
The smoker without other illness
The patient with seasonal allergies
The patient in her third trimester of pregnancy
The marathon runner

explain.html:
Most Coccidioides infections stay mild: about 60% are asymptomatic, 30% mild to moderate, 5 to 10% complicated, and under 1% fatal. The question in a desert clinic is who is likely to fall into the small group with disseminated disease. The listed risk factors for dissemination are immunosuppression, organ transplantation, lymphoma, HIV/AIDS, steroid therapy, diabetes, third-trimester pregnancy and male gender. When it spreads, it most often reaches the skin, bones, joints and meninges.

Among these five patients, only the woman in her third trimester carries one of those risks. Being a student, a runner, a smoker with no other illness, or having seasonal allergies is not on the list, so she is the one who needs closer follow-up.
explain.table:
Valley fever outcomeShare of cases
AsymptomaticAbout 60%
Mild to moderateAbout 30%
Complicated5 to 10%
FatalUnder 1%
why: Being a student carries no specific risk for dissemination.
Smoking alone is not on the list of risk factors for dissemination.
Seasonal allergies do not impair the immunity that contains this fungus.
Athletic training is not a risk factor for dissemination.
explain.takeaway: Disseminated coccidioidomycosis is more likely with immunosuppression, transplantation, lymphoma, HIV, steroids, diabetes, third-trimester pregnancy and male sex.

explain.objective: Introduce examples of common human pathogens with clinical correlates

rows.if_right: a smoker who has also had an organ transplant

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old gardener has a small papule on the back of his hand that appeared about 2 weeks after he was scratched while handling moss and plant stakes. The papule has ulcerated, and several similar nodules have since appeared in a line running up his forearm. He has no fever and feels well. Culture of a biopsy grows a fungus that is a mold at room temperature and a yeast at body temperature.

Which treatment is preferred for this infection?
choices: Caspofungin
No therapy, since these lesions always resolve
Itraconazole
Topical terbinafine
Intravenous amphotericin B with flucytosine

explain.html:
Subcutaneous mycoses start when soil or plant fungi are pushed beneath the skin through a wound, as hyphae or spores. Sporothrix schenckii is one of them and is also a dimorphic fungus: a mold at room temperature and a yeast at body temperature. It lives in soil, moss and vegetation and infects people through inoculation into the skin, usually during gardening or landscaping. Days to weeks later a papule forms at the site and usually ulcerates. Similar lesions then appear along the lymphatic channels leading away from it. Diagnosis is by culture, and itraconazole is the treatment of choice for cutaneous and osteoarticular disease.

This gardener was scratched handling moss, then developed an ulcerated papule and a line of nodules up the forearm. A mold-to-yeast culture confirms Sporothrix.
explain.table:
ClassTargetExample
PolyenesInsert into the membrane and raise its permeabilityAmphotericin B
AzolesC14-alpha-demethylation of lanosterol (ergosterol synthesis)Fluconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole
Echinocandins1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase (cell wall)Caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin
AllylaminesSqualene epoxidase (ergosterol synthesis)Terbinafine
Pyrimidine analogsConverted to 5-fluorouracil, blocks DNA and RNA synthesisFlucytosine
why: Caspofungin, an echinocandin, is first-line for candidemia, not sporotrichosis.
These lesions keep spreading along lymphatics and need treatment.
Topical therapy treats dermatophytes in keratinized skin, not a subcutaneous infection tracking along lymphatics.
Amphotericin B with flucytosine is the induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis.
explain.takeaway: Sporothrix schenckii, a dimorphic fungus inoculated from plants or soil, causes nodules along lymphatics and is treated with itraconazole.

questions.stem:
Four clinical isolates are examined. Isolate W is unicellular, spherical, and reproduces by budding. Isolate X is multicellular, grows by longitudinal extension of hyphae, and produces spores. Isolate Y grows as a mold on a plate at room temperature but as a yeast in tissue at body temperature. Isolate Z was recovered from skin scrapings and digests keratin.

Which assignment is correct?
choices: Y is best classified by site of infection rather than morphology
Z is a systemic mycosis acquired by spore inhalation
W is Aspergillus and X is Candida
Y could be Histoplasma or Blastomyces
X is Cryptococcus and W is Mucor

explain.html:
Fungi are classified three ways: by morphology (yeast, mold, dimorphic), by site or depth of infection (cutaneous, mucosal, subcutaneous, systemic) and by epidemiology (opportunistic, healthcare associated, endemic). By morphology, yeasts are unicellular, spherical to elliptical cells that reproduce by budding, such as Candida and Cryptococcus. Molds are multicellular hyphae that grow by longitudinal extension and produce spores, such as Aspergillus and the agents of mucormycosis. Dimorphic fungi switch between yeast and mold with temperature or environment; they include Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides and Sporothrix.

Isolate Y is a mold on the plate and a yeast in tissue, so it is dimorphic and could be Histoplasma or Blastomyces. W is a yeast, X is a mold, and Z is a keratin-digesting dermatophyte.
explain.table:
MorphologyDescriptionExamples
YeastUnicellular, reproduces by buddingCandida, Cryptococcus
MoldMulticellular hyphae, produces sporesAspergillus, mucormycosis agents
DimorphicYeast or mold with temperature or environmentHistoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Sporothrix
why: Switching between mold and yeast is a morphologic feature; site of infection is a separate classification.
Digesting keratin from skin scrapings marks a cutaneous dermatophyte, not a systemic mycosis.
Aspergillus is a mold and Candida is a yeast, so this reverses W and X.
Cryptococcus is a yeast and the mucormycosis agents are molds, so both labels are reversed.
explain.takeaway: Fungi are classified by morphology (yeast, mold, dimorphic), by site or depth of infection, and by epidemiology; dimorphic fungi include Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides and Sporothrix.

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old farm worker who usually goes barefoot has a chronically swollen, deformed foot with multiple draining sinus tracts that have developed slowly over several years. Imaging shows involvement of the underlying bone. He recalls a minor puncture injury before the swelling began. He has no fever and no systemic symptoms.

Which route of acquisition explains this infection?
choices: Spread through the bloodstream from an intravascular catheter
Person-to-person contact with infected skin and hair
Reactivation of a latent intracellular infection
Inhalation of airborne conidia into the lungs
Inoculation of soil organisms through a minor wound

explain.html:
Subcutaneous mycoses are infections beneath the skin caused by soil and plant fungi whose hyphae or spores get into wounds. The classic example is mycetoma, a chronic infection of the skin, subcutaneous tissue and sometimes bone. It usually involves the foot, where the swollen, draining limb is called watering can foot. Several fungi or actinomycetes can cause it, and in each case the organism is inoculated into the skin by a minor injury, then spreads slowly through local tissue. This route sets it apart from systemic mycoses, which are inhaled, and from dermatophytes, which spread by contact.

This barefoot farm worker has a deformed foot with draining sinuses and bone involvement that developed over years after a puncture wound. That is mycetoma acquired by inoculation.
explain.table:
DepthHow it is acquiredExample
CutaneousDirect contact with infected hair and skinTinea (dermatophytes)
SubcutaneousInoculation of soil or plant fungi through a woundMycetoma, sporotrichosis
SystemicInhalation of spores or entry into the bloodstreamHistoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, candidemia
why: Spread through the blood from a catheter describes candidemia.
Person-to-person contact with skin and hair is how dermatophytes spread.
This is a primary inoculation infection, not reactivation of a latent one.
Inhaled conidia cause systemic mycoses that begin in the lungs.
explain.takeaway: Mycetoma is a chronic subcutaneous mycosis of the foot, sometimes reaching bone, caused by soil fungi or actinomycetes inoculated through a minor wound.

explain.objective: Introduce examples of common human pathogens with clinical correlates

rows.why: This is a primary inoculation infection, not reactivation of a latent one.
rows.if_right: an old lung infection that returned when the patient became immunosuppressed

rows.why: Inhaled conidia cause systemic mycoses that begin in the lungs.

questions.stem:
Two antifungal drugs are tested on the same fungus. With drug 1, squalene accumulates in the cell and no squalene epoxide is formed. With drug 2, lanosterol accumulates and the cell cannot complete the final sterol of its membrane. Both drugs ultimately reduce the same membrane component.

Which membrane component is depleted by both drugs?
choices: Chitin
Beta-D-glucan
Cholesterol
Mannoprotein
Ergosterol

explain.html:
The fungal cell membrane uses ergosterol as its sterol, where human membranes use cholesterol. Ergosterol is made through a pathway that runs from squalene to squalene epoxide to lanosterol and finally to ergosterol. Two drug classes block steps along it. Allylamines such as terbinafine inhibit squalene epoxidase, so squalene builds up. Azoles such as fluconazole, itraconazole and posaconazole inhibit C14-alpha-demethylation of lanosterol, so lanosterol builds up. Amphotericin B hits the same molecule from another direction by binding the membrane and raising its permeability.

Drug 1 leaves squalene unconverted and drug 2 leaves lanosterol unconverted. Both blocks sit on the same pathway, so both deplete ergosterol from the membrane.
explain.table:
ClassTargetExample
PolyenesInsert into the membrane and raise its permeabilityAmphotericin B
AzolesC14-alpha-demethylation of lanosterol (ergosterol synthesis)Fluconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole
Echinocandins1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase (cell wall)Caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin
AllylaminesSqualene epoxidase (ergosterol synthesis)Terbinafine
Pyrimidine analogsConverted to 5-fluorouracil, blocks DNA and RNA synthesisFlucytosine
why: Chitin is a wall polymer and is not made through the squalene to lanosterol pathway.
Beta-D-glucan is a wall component and the target of echinocandins, not of these two sterol-pathway drugs.
Cholesterol is the human membrane sterol; the fungal end product of this pathway is ergosterol.
Mannoproteins are surface wall proteins unrelated to squalene epoxidase or lanosterol demethylase.
explain.takeaway: Allylamines (squalene epoxidase) and azoles (lanosterol C14-alpha-demethylation) both deplete ergosterol, the sterol of the fungal membrane.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the components of a fungal cell

rows.if_right: glucose polymers no longer being incorporated into the wall

questions.stem:
A 57-year-old man with advanced untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection has 2 weeks of pain on swallowing and a sensation of food sticking, with weight loss from reduced intake. White patches are seen on the tongue and buccal mucosa. Upper endoscopy shows white plaques and shallow ulcerations, and biopsy shows budding yeast with pseudohyphae.

Which underlying change best explains why this organism became invasive in him?
choices: Iron overload treated with deferoxamine
Loss of the skin barrier at an inoculation site
Impaired cell-mediated immunity
Deficiency of terminal complement components
Prolonged severe neutropenia from chemotherapy

explain.html:
Candida is a commensal yeast of the mucosal surfaces, and mucosal candidiasis appears when one of two things changes. The first is a disturbance of local ecology, as with antibiotics, steroids or dental devices. The second is impaired immunity, as with immunosuppressive therapy, diabetes or HIV infection. The sites are oral (thrush), esophageal and vaginal. On biopsy the organism is budding yeast with or without pseudohyphae.

This man has untreated advanced HIV with thrush and painful swallowing from esophageal plaques, so the relevant defect is impaired cell-mediated immunity. That loss lets a normally harmless surface yeast invade the mucosa.
why: Deferoxamine therapy for iron overload is a risk factor for mucormycosis.
A break in the skin is how subcutaneous mycoses such as mycetoma begin, not oral and esophageal infection.
Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to bacterial infections, not mucosal yeast.
Prolonged neutropenia from chemotherapy is the classic setting for invasive aspergillosis, not thrush in untreated HIV.
explain.takeaway: Mucosal candidiasis follows disturbed local flora or impaired immunity; in advanced HIV it reflects loss of cell-mediated immunity.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 62-year-old woman with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia receiving chemotherapy has 2 days of cough, hemoptysis, fever, and worsening dyspnea. She is tachypneic, with decreased breath sounds and a pleural friction rub on the right. Chest computed tomography shows several nodules with surrounding ground-glass rings. Bronchoscopy shows necrotic tissue, and histology shows septate hyphae branching at acute angles.

Which property of this organism best explains the necrosis and the imaging findings?
choices: Release of keratinase into surrounding tissue
Conversion to a thick-walled spherule filled with endospores
Invasion of blood vessels with distal infarction
Growth inside macrophages after phagocytosis
Formation of a thick polysaccharide capsule

explain.html:
Aspergillus is a ubiquitous mold that forms septate hyphae with dichotomous branching at acute (45 degree) angles. It causes a spectrum from localized lung disease to disseminated infection. Invasive disease occurs mainly with prolonged, profound neutropenia and transplant immunosuppression. The organism is angioinvasive: it grows into blood vessels and infarcts the tissue beyond them. On CT this produces nodules surrounded by a ring of hemorrhage, the halo sign, and clinically it causes hemoptysis and necrotic lung.

This woman on chemotherapy for leukemia has hemoptysis, nodules with ground-glass rings and septate acute-angle hyphae in necrotic tissue. Vessel invasion with distal infarction explains both the necrosis and the imaging.
explain.table:
Aspergillus syndromeHostKey findingsTreatment
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosisAsthma or cystic fibrosisFleeting infiltrates, eosinophilia, high IgESteroids plus itraconazole or voriconazole
Aspergilloma (fungus ball)Pre-existing cavity, not immunosuppressedRound mass inside a cavity, hemoptysisNone if stable; resection for hemoptysis
Invasive aspergillosisProlonged profound neutropenia, transplantNodules, halo sign, infarctionAntifungal therapy
why: Keratinase is made by dermatophytes and confines them to skin, hair and nails.
Thick-walled spherules with endospores are the tissue form of Coccidioides.
Growth inside macrophages describes Histoplasma, a small yeast, not septate hyphae.
A polysaccharide capsule is the virulence factor of Cryptococcus, a yeast.
explain.takeaway: Aspergillus forms septate, acute-angle hyphae and is angioinvasive, causing infarction, hemoptysis and the CT halo sign in neutropenic hosts.

questions.stem:
A 27-year-old woman with long-standing asthma has worsening wheeze and cough despite her usual inhalers. Chest imaging over several months shows infiltrates that appear in one area and then resolve and appear elsewhere. Laboratory studies show peripheral eosinophilia, a markedly elevated serum immunoglobulin E level, and serum precipitating antibodies to a mold; skin testing to the same mold antigen is reactive.

Which treatment approach fits this condition?
choices: Surgical resection of the involved lobe
Steroids to control inflammation, with an antifungal agent
Observation alone, since the process always resolves
Combined antifungal therapy and aggressive surgical debridement
Topical terbinafine applied to the affected area

explain.html:
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus colonizing the larger airways, and it appears in patients with chronic asthma or cystic fibrosis. The fungus does not invade tissue; the damage comes from the immune response to it. Its cardinal features are asthma-like symptoms, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, peripheral eosinophilia, high serum IgE, serum precipitating antibodies to Aspergillus and skin test reactivity. Exacerbations are treated with steroids to control inflammation and limit lung damage, combined with itraconazole or voriconazole.

This woman has long-standing asthma, infiltrates that come and go, eosinophilia, very high IgE and both precipitins and skin reactivity to the mold. Because the process is immunologic, steroids plus an azole is the fitting approach.
explain.table:
Aspergillus syndromeHostKey findingsTreatment
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosisAsthma or cystic fibrosisFleeting infiltrates, eosinophilia, high IgESteroids plus itraconazole or voriconazole
Aspergilloma (fungus ball)Pre-existing cavity, not immunosuppressedRound mass inside a cavity, hemoptysisNone if stable; resection for hemoptysis
Invasive aspergillosisProlonged profound neutropenia, transplantNodules, halo sign, infarctionAntifungal therapy
why: Resection is used for hemoptysis from an aspergilloma, not for an airway hypersensitivity process.
Untreated exacerbations can cause lasting lung damage, so observation alone is not appropriate.
Antifungals plus aggressive surgical debridement is the approach to mucormycosis.
Topical terbinafine treats cutaneous dermatophyte infection, not an airway disease.
explain.takeaway: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in asthma or cystic fibrosis shows fleeting infiltrates, eosinophilia and high IgE, and is treated with steroids plus an azole.

questions.stem:
A 51-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents after 2 days of headache, facial pain, and nosebleeds. He now has proptosis of the right eye, periorbital swelling, and reduced vision. Examination of the palate shows a black area of dead tissue. Biopsy shows broad, irregular, ribbon-like hyphae without septa that branch at right angles. Blood cultures are negative.

Which management approach is most appropriate?
choices: Observation with repeat imaging in 2 weeks
Removal of any intravascular catheters and oral fluconazole
Steroids to reduce the periorbital inflammation
Antifungal therapy alone, since the blood cultures are negative
Antifungal therapy combined with prompt surgical debridement

explain.html:
Mucormycosis is caused by molds (most often Rhizopus and Mucor) that form broad, irregular, ribbon-like aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching. Patients with uncontrolled diabetes or ketoacidosis are uniquely susceptible, along with those with hematologic malignancy, transplantation or deferoxamine therapy. The most common form is rhinocerebral, spreading from the sinuses behind the orbit into the brain with headache, nosebleeds, proptosis and loss of vision. A black eschar on the nose or palate is pathognomonic, and blood cultures are usually negative. The infection is rapidly fatal, so therapy has to be combined medical and surgical: antifungal drugs plus timely, aggressive debridement that often needs repeating.

This diabetic man has every feature, so drugs alone are not enough.
explain.table:
FeatureMucormycosis agentsAspergillus
HyphaeBroad, ribbon-like, aseptateNarrow, septate
BranchingRight angleAcute (45 degree)
Classic hostUncontrolled diabetes, ketoacidosisProfound neutropenia
TreatmentAntifungal plus aggressive debridementAntifungal therapy
why: This infection can be fatal within days, so waiting two weeks is unsafe.
Catheter removal and fluconazole address candidemia, not a mold invading the sinuses.
Steroids worsen immune function and do not treat the infection.
Negative blood cultures are expected in mucormycosis, and drugs alone are not enough.
explain.takeaway: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis (aseptate, right-angle hyphae and a black eschar in uncontrolled diabetes) needs antifungal therapy plus prompt, repeated surgical debridement.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man with untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection has 1 week of headache, fever, photophobia, neck stiffness, and confusion. Lumbar puncture shows a high opening pressure and 4 leukocytes per microliter, all lymphocytes. A stain of the cerebrospinal fluid mixed with India ink shows round cells surrounded by a wide clear halo.

The clear halo seen around these cells corresponds to which structure, and what is its role?
choices: A sterol-depleted membrane caused by prior drug therapy
A ring of endospores waiting to be released
A chitin-rich wall that resists enzymatic digestion
A polysaccharide capsule that impairs phagocytosis
A layer of host antibody bound to the surface

explain.html:
Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast that is usually inhaled first, often from pigeon droppings, and causes a lung infection. When cell-mediated immunity fails, as in untreated HIV, it spreads through the blood and most often causes meningitis. Cerebrospinal fluid typically shows a high opening pressure with few cells, mostly lymphocytes. India ink is a negative stain: the ink particles cannot get into the thick capsule, so the capsule shows up as a clear halo around each yeast. That polysaccharide capsule is the organism's virulence factor and impairs phagocytosis.

This man with untreated HIV has headache, fever and confusion, a high opening pressure, 4 lymphocytes, and round cells with wide halos on India ink.
explain.table:
OrganismForm in tissueClassic clue
CandidaBudding yeast with pseudohyphaeThrush, candidemia with catheters
CryptococcusEncapsulated yeast (halo on India ink)Meningitis in impaired cell-mediated immunity
HistoplasmaSmall yeast inside macrophagesOhio and Mississippi valleys, bat and bird feces
BlastomycesLarge yeast with broad-based budGreat Lakes, skin lesions
CoccidioidesSpherules filled with endosporesSouthwest deserts, Valley fever
AspergillusSeptate hyphae, acute-angle branchingNeutropenia, angioinvasion, halo sign
Mucormycosis agentsBroad aseptate hyphae, right-angle branchingUncontrolled diabetes, black eschar
why: Drug effects on membrane sterols do not create a clear zone around the cell.
Endospores held inside a thick wall describe the Coccidioides spherule in tissue.
The fungal wall lies inside the capsule, so it is not the wide zone India ink leaves unstained.
Host antibody bound to the surface does not form a wide clear halo on India ink.
explain.takeaway: Cryptococcus has a polysaccharide capsule, seen as a clear halo on India ink, that impairs phagocytosis and drives meningitis when cell-mediated immunity fails.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old missionary returns from Central America with fever, weight loss, and confusion. The liver and spleen are enlarged. Blood counts show pancytopenia. A bone marrow aspirate stained with Wright-Giemsa shows numerous small oval organisms packed inside macrophages, and a silver stain of the same aspirate confirms them. Chest imaging shows findings that the radiologist says could be mistaken for tuberculosis.

Which organism is most likely responsible?
choices: Blastomyces dermatitidis
Coccidioides immitis
Candida glabrata
Sporothrix schenckii
Histoplasma capsulatum

explain.html:
Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus found in the Mississippi and Ohio river valleys, and it is acquired by inhaling airborne conidia from soil enriched with bat and bird feces. In the body the yeast lives and multiplies within macrophages, which carries it to the liver, spleen and bone marrow. It usually involves the lungs but can affect every organ. Symptoms are vague (fever, chills, sweats, fatigue), and it resembles tuberculosis clinically and on imaging. Disseminated disease causes high fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia.

In this missionary, the decisive finding is the marrow aspirate: many small oval yeast packed inside macrophages, confirmed by silver stain. That intracellular yeast form identifies Histoplasma.

questions.stem:
A 32-year-old woman who moved to Arizona 6 weeks ago for work has 2 weeks of fever, cough, fatigue, and aching in several joints. She spent long hours outdoors in dusty conditions. Temperature is 38.3 C (101 F), and scattered wheezes are heard. Tender nodules are present on the extensor surfaces of her arms and legs. Chest imaging shows an infiltrate on one side with a small effusion. Blood counts show leukocytosis with elevated eosinophils.

In tissue, the responsible organism appears in which form?
choices: Small yeast within macrophages
Encapsulated yeast cells with narrow-based budding
Thick-walled spherules filled with endospores
Yeast with a single broad-based bud
Septate hyphae branching at acute angles

explain.html:
Coccidioides immitis and C. posadasii live in dry alkaline soils of the southwestern deserts (San Joaquin Valley, Tucson, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Utah). They are dimorphic in a distinctive way. In soil they grow as filaments that reproduce by forming arthrospores, which the wind carries and people inhale. In tissue they form thick-walled spherules filled with endospores. Most infections are asymptomatic; symptomatic Valley fever brings chest pain, fever, cough, extreme fatigue and painful nodules on the extensor surfaces. Joint pain is common enough to earn the name desert rheumatism.

This woman recently moved to Arizona, spent hours in dust, and has pneumonia, joint aches, extensor nodules and eosinophilia. That is acute Valley fever, and the tissue form is the spherule.

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old logger who works in forests near the Great Lakes has 3 weeks of cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss, with exposure to soil and decaying organic matter. Breath sounds are decreased over the right upper chest, and chest imaging shows a right upper lobe infiltrate. Bronchoscopy with histopathology shows large yeast forms with a single bud attached across a broad base.

If this infection spreads beyond the lungs, which site is most commonly involved?
choices: Skin
Meninges
Heart valves
Thyroid gland
Peripheral nerves

explain.html:
Blastomyces dermatitidis is a dimorphic fungus of the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys, the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River. It is acquired by inhaling spores from soil and decaying organic matter, and it primarily involves the lungs, with weight loss, fever, cough, bloody sputum and chest pain. In tissue it appears as a large yeast with a single broad-based bud. Beyond the lungs it can spread to the skin, bones and urogenital tract. The skin is the second most frequent site, and skin lesions are the most common sign of disseminated disease. They range from papules and nodules to ulcers, abscesses and draining lesions.

This logger from the Great Lakes has a right upper lobe infiltrate with broad-based budding yeast, so the most likely site of spread is the skin.

Valve infection is typical of bacteria and of candidemia, not of blastomycosis.
No fungus in this block is tied to thyroid spread; blastomycosis spreads to skin, bone and the urogenital tract.
Peripheral nerve damage is not a feature of blastomycosis.
explain.takeaway: Blastomyces dermatitidis forms large broad-based budding yeast and, after the lungs, most often spreads to the skin, then bone and urogenital tract.
